scenes.title: Watch the whole motion first

beats.text: Consider a crate on a rough ramp. A rope tugs it up the ramp, at an angle... but only gently. Held there, the crate stays put.
Now the worker lets go. The rope keeps tugging the same way, but the crate begins to slide... down the ramp.
Friction fights the slide, so it acts up the ramp. The crate speeds up slowly, not freely.
How quickly does it gain speed? For that we need every force along the ramp, and across it.

scenes.title: Two directions: along and perpendicular

beats.text: On a slope, forget horizontal and vertical. Use two directions: along the slope, and perpendicular to it.
The weight still acts straight down. The angle between it and the perpendicular is the slope angle, theta, so the part into the slope is m g cos theta.
beats.ink: into the slope: mg cos θ

beats.text: And the part down the slope is m g sine theta.
beats.ink: down the slope: mg sin θ

beats.text: Perpendicular to the slope nothing moves, so R balances those forces. With nothing else pulling that way, R equals m g cos theta. A rope at an angle changes that.
beats.ink: no other ⊥ force: R = mg cos θ

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The full question. A crate of mass four kilograms sits on a rough ramp at thirty degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is zero point two five. Take g as ten.
A rope pulls the crate with a force of eight newtons, at thirty degrees above the ramp, pointing up the ramp.
The crate is released from rest, and stays in contact with the ramp.
Find the normal reaction, the maximum friction, which way the crate moves, and its acceleration.
Before any calculation: will the rope drag it up, or will it slide down? Take a moment.

scenes.title: Resolve along and perpendicular to the ramp

beats.text: First the weight: four times ten, forty newtons, straight down. Draw its triangle against the slope.
Into the slope: m g cos theta. Forty cos thirty is twenty root three, about thirty-four point six newtons.
Down the slope: m g sine theta. Forty sine thirty is twenty newtons.
Now the rope: eight newtons at thirty degrees above the slope. Its triangle sits on the slope direction.
Along the slope, upwards: eight cos thirty, four root three, about six point nine three newtons.
Away from the slope: eight sine thirty, four newtons.
These four parts now replace the weight and the rope. Never count a force and its parts together.

scenes.title: The normal reaction, then the limit

beats.text: Perpendicular to the slope nothing moves, so those forces balance: R, plus the rope’s four newtons, minus m g cos theta, equals zero.
So R is twenty root three minus four: about thirty point six newtons. Smaller than m g cos theta, because the rope lifts a little.
The most friction this ramp can give: f max equals mu R.
Zero point two five times thirty point six... about seven point six six newtons.

scenes.title: Which way does it go?

beats.text: Along the slope, ignore friction for a moment. Down: twenty newtons from the weight. Up: six point nine three from the rope. Down wins, by thirteen point one newtons.
Can friction hold thirteen point one? Its limit is seven point six six. No. So the crate slides down, and friction acts up the slope, at its maximum.
Watch: released from rest, it starts to move down the ramp.

scenes.title: Newton’s second law along the ramp

beats.text: Take down the slope as positive. Resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Weight part, minus the rope part, minus friction, equals four a.

scenes.title: What if the rope pulled along the ramp?

beats.text: What if the rope pulled along the ramp instead? No perpendicular part, so R equals m g cos theta: about thirty-four point six newtons.
Then f max is zero point two five times that: about eight point six six newtons. More grip, and all eight newtons pull up the slope.
